nodes.title: Fever in Children Under 5
nodes.summary: This section provides comprehensive guidance for fever in children under 5, covering initial assessment with risk stratification, necessary investigations, appropriate antimicrobial treatment guidelines, supportive care like antipyretics, and detailed discharge instructions including safety netting.

children.title: Fever in Children Under 5 — Overview
children.summary: This document is a synthetic test document and explicitly states it is not clinical guidance. It contains plausible recommendations for indexing and retrieval pipeline testing purposes only.
children.content:
> **SYNTHETIC TEST DOCUMENT — NOT CLINICAL GUIDANCE.** Written to exercise the
> ingest, indexing and retrieval pipeline. The recommendations below are
> plausible in shape but must never be used for patient care.

children.title: Initial Assessment
children.summary: This section covers initial fever assessment in children under 5 by defining fever and emphasizing overall status over temperature alone. It details risk stratification using Green, Amber, and Red traffic light categories, and lists specific red flags requiring immediate escalation.

children.title: Initial Assessment — Overview
children.summary: This passage defines fever (38.0°C or above) and notes that this is a red flag for children under 3 months. It instructs recording vital signs and emphasizes assessing overall child status over fever height alone.
children.content:
Fever is defined as a temperature of 38.0°C or above measured at the axilla or
tympanic membrane. In children under 3 months a temperature of 38.0°C or above
is treated as a red flag on its own and warrants immediate senior review.

Record temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, capillary refill time and
conscious level at first contact. Do not rely on the height of the fever alone
to judge severity — a child with a temperature of 40°C who is alert and playing
is at lower risk than a drowsy child at 38.2°C.

children.title: Traffic Light Categories
children.summary: This passage details three traffic light categories for assessing fever in children under 5 years old: Green (low risk) with normal signs, Amber (intermediate risk) with specific concerning features like pallor or dry membranes, and Red (high risk) with severe indicators such as mottled skin or tachypnoea.
children.content:
Green (low risk) children have normal colour, respond normally to social cues,
have moist mucous membranes and no red or amber features.

Amber (intermediate risk) features include pallor reported by the parent,
reduced activity, nasal flaring, dry mucous membranes, poor feeding in infants,
reduced urine output, or a fever of 5 days or longer.

Red (high risk) features include mottled or blue skin, no response to social
cues, a weak or continuous cry, grunting, tachypnoea above 60 breaths per
minute, reduced skin turgor, or a non-blanching rash.

children.title: Red Flags Requiring Immediate Escalation
children.summary: This passage lists specific signs requiring immediate escalation for fever in children under 5. These red flags include a non-blanching rash, neck stiffness, status epilepticus, focal neurological signs, or a bulging fontanelle.
children.content:
A non-blanching rash, neck stiffness, status epilepticus, focal neurological
signs or a bulging fontanelle require immediate escalation and empirical
treatment before investigations are complete.

children.title: Investigations
children.summary: This passage details specific investigations for fever in children under 5, including required tests like full blood count and urine culture. It outlines indications for lumbar puncture and chest radiography, and mandates urine testing for young children with fever.
children.content:
Children with any red feature require full blood count, C-reactive protein,
blood culture, blood gas and urine culture. Lumbar puncture is indicated in all
infants under 1 month with fever, in infants 1–3 months who appear unwell, and
in any child with reduced conscious level.

Chest radiography is not routine. Reserve it for children with oxygen
saturation below 92%, tachypnoea out of proportion to fever, or focal chest
signs on examination.

Urine testing is mandatory in every child under 3 years with fever and no
obvious source, because urinary tract infection is common and frequently
presents without localising symptoms at this age.

children.title: Antimicrobial Treatment
children.summary: This section covers when and how to use antimicrobial treatment for fever in children under 5. It details age-specific empiric regimens, weight-based dosing guidelines for specific antibiotics, and advises against unnecessary antibiotic use for common viral illnesses.

children.title: Empiric Therapy by Age
children.summary: This passage details empiric antimicrobial therapy for fever in children under 5 based on age groups. It specifies drug regimens including cefotaxime plus amoxicillin for infants under 1 month, ceftriaxone with optional amoxicillin for 1-3 months, and ceftriaxone with potential vancomycin addition for older, high-risk children.
children.content:
Infants under 1 month receive intravenous cefotaxime plus amoxicillin, the
amoxicillin covering Listeria monocytogenes, which is not reliably treated by
cephalosporins alone.

Infants of 1–3 months receive intravenous ceftriaxone, with amoxicillin added
if the child appears unwell or if Listeria cannot be excluded on clinical
grounds.

Children over 3 months with a high-risk presentation receive intravenous
ceftriaxone. Add vancomycin where meningitis is suspected and local pneumococcal
resistance exceeds 5%.

children.title: Weight-Based Dosing
children.summary: This passage details weight-based dosing for ceftriaxone (80 mg/kg daily), cefotaxime (50 mg/kg every 6 hours in neonates), and amoxicillin for suspected Listeria (50 mg/kg every 8 hours). It emphasizes calculating all pediatric doses using current weight.
children.content:
Ceftriaxone is dosed at 80 mg/kg once daily to a maximum of 4 g. Cefotaxime is
dosed at 50 mg/kg every 6 hours in the neonatal period. Amoxicillin for
suspected Listeria is 50 mg/kg every 8 hours.

Every paediatric dose must be calculated on an accurate current weight, not an
estimate from age, and checked by a second practitioner before administration.

children.title: When Not to Give Antibiotics
children.summary: The passage advises against prescribing antibiotics for common childhood illnesses like viral infections, otitis media with effusion, uncomplicated upper respiratory tract infections, or fever alone in well children. It notes that most febrile children under 5 have self-limiting viral causes.
children.content:
The majority of febrile children under 5 have a self-limiting viral illness.
Children in the green category with an identified viral source do not need
antibiotics, and prescribing them drives resistance without shortening the
illness.

Do not prescribe antibiotics for otitis media with effusion, for uncomplicated
upper respiratory tract infection, or for fever alone in a well child.

children.title: Antipyretics and Supportive Care
children.summary: The passage advises on using paracetamol (15 mg/kg) or ibuprofen (10 mg/kg) for fever relief in children under 5, while also recommending oral fluids and advising against tepid sponging or improper dressing.
children.content:
Paracetamol at 15 mg/kg every 4–6 hours or ibuprofen at 10 mg/kg every 6–8
hours may be used to relieve distress. Do not use them solely to reduce
temperature in a comfortable child, and do not alternate the two agents
routinely.

Encourage oral fluids. Do not use tepid sponging, and do not underdress or
overwrap a febrile child.

children.title: Discharge and Safety Netting
children.summary: This passage outlines discharge instructions for children with fever under 5. It specifies warning signs requiring reassessment (e.g., non-blanching rash, drowsiness) and mandates a review within 24 hours for those discharged with amber features.
children.content:
Children in the green category may be managed at home. Give the parent verbal
and written advice describing the warning signs that require reassessment: a
non-blanching rash, reduced fluid intake, drowsiness, or fever persisting beyond
5 days.

Arrange review within 24 hours for any child discharged with amber features, and
document who will perform that review.
